items.title: Nova Scotia business accused of buying illegal lobster denies allegations
items.description: One of the Nova Scotia businesses accused of buying illegally caught lobsters in the province denies any allegations of wrongdoing.

items._ogDesc: One of the Nova Scotia businesses accused of buying illegally caught lobsters in the province denies any allegations of wrongdoing.
items.body:
LOCKEPORT — One of the Nova Scotia businesses accused of buying illegally caught lobsters in the province denies any allegations of wrongdoing.

The Nova Scotia government announced Friday that charges have been laid against two businesses in the southwestern part of the province under the Fisheries and Coastal Resources Act.

Independent Fisheries Ltd. in Lockeport, N.S., and a numbered company in Shelburne County are both facing charges of buying, selling or processing fish that were caught without a valid licence.

A spokesperson for Independent Fisheries denies the allegations, saying the firm operates with a robust due diligence process that ensures lobster is sourced in-season from legal license holders, and they require proof of origin for every transaction.

The company says it looks forward to being vindicated through the legal process.

The numbered company, 3329874 Nova Scotia Ltd., could not be reached.

The cases are scheduled for a court date in Yarmouth Provincial Court next month.

The president of the Unified Fisheries Conservation Alliance said Friday the organization is pleased charges have been laid.

The group that represents thousands of independent, multi-species commercial fishers and associations across the Maritimes filed a lawsuit against Independent Fisheries Ltd. in November 2024.

A court hearing about the lawsuit was held last month, but there hasn’t been a ruling yet.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 17, 2026.

items.body:
Stellantis workers in Canada begin voting today on whether to give their union a strike mandate as collective bargaining negotiations remain stalled.

The two-day votes will wrap up tomorrow, with Unifor set to announce results on Monday.

Unifor says potential strike action remains its last resort as it still hopes to reach a negotiated deal with the company.

However, the union remains at loggerheads with the automaker after Stellantis announced plans to sell its idled Brampton, Ont., assembly plant to defence contractor Roshel.

Stellantis says market and trade conditions have hurt the business case for keeping the plant, but that the move to sell could support future jobs there.

More than 2,000 workers were laid off from the Brampton plant when it halted operations in 2023, as Stellantis later moved production of its Jeep Compass from the site to Illinois.

items._ogDesc: Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem is warning that persistently high global energy prices will drive up the outlook for inflation at home.
items.body:
Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem is warning that persistently high global energy prices will drive up the outlook for inflation at home.

While Macklem said global resilience is being tested after a series of shocks, he also expressed some confidence in Canada’s ability to weather the storm.

The head of the Bank of Canada spoke to reporters on Saturday in a press conference from the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund meetings in Bangkok.

He said the prevailing message from his peers at the summit is that the global economy has been performing better than expected in the face of ongoing wars in Iran and Ukraine, sweeping trade disruptions and higher borrowing costs from rising bond yields.

But Macklem also said that resilience is increasingly “under strain” as shocks like the Middle East conflict persist and drive up energy prices.

Some of those sources of resilience -- like releasing global oil reserves -- are being depleted, he said.

“You can only release strategic energy, oil reserves so many times, but that has helped contain this energy price shock,” Macklem said.

The war in the Middle East is also spreading in the form of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. Macklem said that escalation, combined with damage to refining capacity in the Gulf region and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, means there’s no relief in sight for global oil prices.

Those global forces feed through into the prices Canadians pay at home for gasoline, diesel and heating oil.

The Bank of Canada will release updated forecasts for the economy and inflation alongside its interest rate decision on Oct. 28.

The central bank is mandated to keep inflation at its two per cent target. Inflation in Canada has held at three per cent for two months in a row.

Macklem said he expects that outlook for inflation will be “quite a bit higher” than it was in the central bank’s last forecast in July. That projection had inflation cooling to around 2.5 per cent in the second half of this year.

The Bank of Canada will get a look at how domestic prices are responding to global cost pressures when Statistics Canada releases its September inflation report on Monday.

The central bank raises its policy rate when inflation is likely to stray too far from its two per cent target.

So far, the Bank of Canada has been content to look through near-term inflationary impacts from the war in Iran.

But Macklem has increasingly signalled the central bank is getting worried about inflation and is prepared to react with hikes to its policy rate if monetary policymakers see signs price pressures are spreading.

“The question we’re going to be asking ourselves is, is inflation likely to come back down towards our target on its own, or are we going to have to raise interest rates to influence the path?” he said Saturday.

Despite headwinds facing the economy from U.S. tariffs and global geopolitical instability, Macklem also expressed some confidence in Canada.

He argued relative stability in the value of the Canadian dollar compared to its American counterpart reflects some recent weakness in the U.S. dollar, but also external optimism in Canada.

“Canada is a well-governed, good partner. We’re starting to see some recovery and investment. Companies are adapting to the increased tariff uncertainty. And I think that confidence is reflected,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 17, 2026.

Craig Lord, The Canadian Press

items.title: Canada’s wool industry looks inward after tariffs cut it off from the U.S.
items.description: Canada’s wool sector is in the midst of a transformation as one of the many segments of the economy dealing with tariffs put in place by U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Sheep are pictured in Ferryland, N.L., on Saturday, Oct. 24, 2020. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Paul Daly]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Paul Daly</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Canada’s wool sector is in the midst of a transformation as one of the many segments of the economy dealing with tariffs put in place by U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration.
items.body:
“The King once said that if the smartest scientist with the most well-funded lab was to come up with a miracle fibre, it still wouldn’t be as good as wool for all that it gives us,” says Matthew Rowe.

Rowe is the chairman of the Campaign for Wool in Canada and the Canadian Wool Council (CWC), which advocates for the advancement of the country’s wool industry across its entire value chain.

In an interview with BNN Bloomberg on Thursday, he said Canada’s wool sector is in the midst of a transformation as one of the many segments of the economy dealing with tariffs put in place by U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration.

  • Latest economic news on BNNBloomberg.ca

In August, the U.S. began imposing 50 per cent tariffs on greasy – or raw – wool from Canada, as well as some finished wool products. The move essentially cut off Canadian producers from U.S. buyers, according to Rowe.

“The tariffs are on our raw wool, which really affects our ability to access processing opportunities because there’s parts of our chain that are broken,” he said.

“We’ve traditionally relied on the United States for scouring and other steps to transform [wool] into high value-added products, and the tariffs sort of cut off that option for a lot of companies now.”

For years, Canadian producers have had to ship their wool south of the border to large-scale U.S. processing facilities, which Canada doesn’t have, before taking it back to use in finished products.

Until larger domestic facilities are built, big Canadian wool producers must look to the U.K., the Czech Republic or China for processing if they hope to avoid the steep U.S. tariffs, Rowe explained.

‘Help Canadian wool go global’

The rupture in the Canada-U.S. wool trading relationship has left some Canadian producers frustrated with their American counterparts and unsure when or if there will be a return to normalcy.

  • ‘Now, it’s personal’: Canadian wool and yarn producers walk away from U.S. customers

But the trade tensions have given the industry a renewed focus on finding ways it can expand both domestically and overseas at a time when global wool prices are on the rise, along with demand for sustainable materials.

Earlier this month, the federal government announced an investment of nearly $160,000 over two years to the CWC, “to help Canadian wool go global.”

“Canada has high-quality products, like our Canadian wool, to offer the world, and we want to help get more of them into global markets,” Minister of Agriculture and Agri-Food Heath MacDonald said in an Oct. 7 press release.

“By supporting international promotion and trade, this investment will help our producers and processors expand their reach, overcome market barriers, and capitalize on emerging opportunities around the world.”

‘High-profile endorsement’

Another proponent of Canada’s wool industry is King Charles III, who has campaigned globally for the preservation of traditional materials and craftsmanship, Rowe explained.

“His Majesty is patron of the Campaign for Wool in Canada,” he said. “It’s really helpful to have that kind of high-profile endorsement.”

Rowe said he’s grateful for the support that’s been provided to the industry by the federal government, noting that before the CWC was founded in 2018, “wool hadn’t been funded for generations.”

He said he’d like to see the momentum turned into “significant investment” in Canada’s domestic processing capabilities, specifically the first stage known as scouring, which cleans the wool after it’s been shorn from sheep.

“The first thing you have to do is wash it,” said Rowe.

“From there you can comb it, you can align it in different ways to turn it into yarn, to turn it into felt, the yarn can then become cloth, but it all starts with that large-scale scouring, and that’s something Canada currently lacks.”

items._ogDesc: Ottawa is adding new express entry points for permanent residency applicants in “high-wage” jobs.
items.body:
OTTAWA -- Ottawa is adding new express entry points for some permanent residency applicants in “high-wage” jobs, Immigration Minister Lena Diab said Friday.

The government also plans to remove the requirement for an employer to prove they can’t find a qualified Canadian for those jobs.

The policies, which will take effect on Nov. 3, will apply to applicants who already have Canadian work experience, or who have a job offer in a high-wage field such as engineering.

The government considers a high-wage job one that pays at least 1.3 times the national median wage. The new policy offers more points for an occupation’s wage level, with higher paying jobs being worth more express entry points.

Statistics Canada says the median annual income in Canada in 2024 was $46,300.

The government is also introducing a temporary policy to remove the requirement for an employer to include a Labour Market Impact Assessment for a qualifying job that’s eligible for the new express entry points.

The government says this change is meant to simplify the application process and is part of its efforts over the past year to attract more immigrants in high-paying fields to Canada.

The government has introduced measures to give more express entry points to those working in medicine, the skilled trades, transportation and research.

Permanent residency candidates who are already in the express entry pool will have their scores modified to reflect the new points for Canadian work experience and job offers.

The Immigration Department says it may take up to two weeks for the new totals to be calculated and invitations to apply for permanent residency will be paused during that time.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 16, 2026

David Baxter, The Canadian Press

Correction

This is a corrected version of The Canadian Press story. An earlier version said the national median hourly wage was $55.03.

items._ogDesc: Hitachi Energy has announced a $479-million investment in a new transformer insulation factory, with support from the federal and provincial governments.
items.body:
Amid a trade war with the United States, a global energy company is making a major investment in London, Ont.

Hitachi Energy has announced a $479-million investment in a new transformer insulation factory, with support from the federal and provincial governments.

The 226,000-square-foot (21,000-square-metre) facility will be built at Huron Street and Veterans Memorial Parkway.

“This new facility will create over 100 permanent skilled manufacturing and engineering jobs,” said Carla Vicente of Hitachi Energy Canada.

  • Latest updates on company news here

The federal and provincial governments are contributing a combined $50 million.

“More than 20,000 tonnes of wood fibre will be turned into electric grid pressboard and will strengthen the domestic supply chain and our forest sector,” said federal Industry Minister Melanie Joly at a news conference at the site.

Ontario Economic Development Minister Vic Fedeli said the facility will be the first transformer pressboard factory in Canada and the largest of its kind in the world.

Ontario Energy and Mines Minister Stephen Lecce said global thinking is at the forefront of the investment.

“We’re building an end-to-end supply chain made in Canada, made by Canadians and for Canadians, and I think that is the ultimate illustration of success that we can punch back and stand up for the good of Canada.”

Although construction is underway, the factory is not expected to be ready until late 2028.

The project marks Hitachi Energy’s second venture into London. Last year, the company purchased Canduct Industries, a manufacturer of transformer cooling equipment.

  • Latest economic news on BNNBloomberg.ca

Hitachi Energy executives told CTV News London that site easements and access to electrical power were critical to the final decision to build in the city.

Mayor Josh Morgan echoed the importance of reliable energy infrastructure in attracting major investments.

“Safe, secure, reliable power, and power infrastructure are critical — critical — to these investments.”

Hitachi Energy says the factory remains on track for completion despite potential changes in economic conditions.

“We have a very solid foundation to make sure the factory is ready on time. Hitachi Energy and Hitachi are committed to the long term,” said Bruno Melles, CEO of Hitachi Energy’s Transformers business unit.

THE CANADIAN PRESS/Justin Tang]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Justin Tang</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu said trade talks between Canada and India advanced over the past week as he led a major trade mission to New Delhi, Bengaluru and Mumbai.
items.body:
OTTAWA — International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu said trade talks between Canada and India advanced over the past week as he led a major trade mission to New Delhi, Bengaluru and Mumbai.

A statement from his office said the mission included representatives from nearly 300 Canadian businesses and exporters, and resulted in 34 commercial agreements worth almost $300 million.

It said the agreements spanned multiple sectors, including aerospace, clean technology and energy transitions, information and communications technologies, infrastructure, life sciences and tourism.

Sidhu’s office also said the minister met with Indian Industry Minister Piyush Goyal in both New Delhi and Mumbai to push forward trade talks. Canada and India are looking to conclude negotiations on a new Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement by the end of the year.

The ministers have now met 10 times since May 2025.

Prime Minister Mark Carney and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi formally launched trade negotiations almost a year ago on the sidelines of the G20 leaders’ summit in South Africa.

Carney confirmed on Thursday Modi will visit Toronto and Ottawa on Dec. 11 and 12, just ahead of this year’s G20 summit in Miami.

The Liberals have set out to double non-U.S. exports over the next decade and have also set a goal of doubling two-way trade with India to $70 billion annually by 2030.

In 2025, two-way goods and services trade between Canada and India amounted to $30.4 billion.

In May, Goyal said Carney’s visit to his country paved the way for a complete overhaul of the Canada-India relationship.

Canada and India have been in trade talks since 2010. But those talks were shut down in 2023 after the federal government accused New Delhi of playing a role in the assassination of a Canadian Sikh activist in Surrey, B.C.

Carney, who made resetting relations with India a priority after he became prime minister in 2025, visited Mumbai and New Delhi in March. It was the first visit there by a Canadian prime minister in eight years.

That trip concluded with a meeting with Modi and the signing of a series of agreements — including a $2.6-billion deal to supply India with about 22 million pounds of uranium for energy generation and 10 commercial agreements worth more than $5.5 billion.

“From energy and critical minerals to aerospace, Canadian companies have built valuable connections that will strengthen our long-term partnership with one of the world’s fastest-growing major economies,” Sidhu said in a statement.

“Canada is ready to be the reliable partner India needs, and the opportunities secured on this mission will deliver lasting benefits for our workers and businesses.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 16, 2026

Catherine Morrison, The Canadian Press

items.title: Tesla’s new Roadster car can thrust itself in the air. But don’t expect to drive it anytime soon
items.description: Tesla has unveiled its new Roadster sports car, which can thrust itself in the air, among other engineering bells and whistles. But drivers shouldn’t expect to take it for a spin anytime soon.
items._ogDesc: Tesla has unveiled its new Roadster sports car, which can thrust itself in the air, among other engineering bells and whistles. But drivers shouldn’t expect to take it for a spin anytime soon.
items.body:
CHICAGO — Tesla has unveiled its new Roadster sports car, which can thrust itself in the air, among other engineering bells and whistles. But drivers shouldn’t expect to take it for a spin anytime soon.

Elon Musk’s electric car company rolled out its second-generation Roadster at a Thursday event, showing off a set of cold gas thrusters and a “multi-mode” suction system that can fling the car in the air for short spurts and spin the vehicle mid-flight.

“Turns out the future does have flying cars,” Musk, Tesla’s CEO, wrote on his social media platform X shortly after.

That future could be a ways off, however, given the regulatory hurdles for flying vehicles and the tangle of state rules that still need to be met.

“I’m not sure every state is going to allow a driver in the middle of traffic to suddenly elevate himself and fly,” said David Vladeck, a Georgetown Law professor and former director of the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection. “There is going to be a long process to let anything like that on a road.”

Thursday’s event was hosted at the Texas rocket testing and development center for SpaceX -- Musk’s now publicly-traded rocket company -- and Tesla’s executives noted that they “borrowed” some SpaceX technology to get the new Roadster in the air. Beyond quick jumps and flips, Tesla also said the car can accelerate from zero to 60 miles (96.6 kilometres) an hour in less than a second.

This week’s launch arrived after years of delays and anticipation around the new Roadster -- and Tesla shares climbed in morning trading on Friday before falling amid a sell-off in companies tied to artificial intelligence.

The wait isn’t completely over. Musk said production for consumers won’t begin until 2028. Tesla also didn’t immediately set a price tag on its latest EV.

Tesla was taking reservations for Roadster “rocket” car purchases on its website Friday morning, though the fine print said there was no guarantee when the vehicle would be delivered -- or whether it would be delivered at all.

Bryant Walker Smith, former vice chair of a Department of Transportation advisory group on innovation, was unimpressed -- though he did note Musk’s ability to keep Tesla’s stock high.

“This was a demonstration of a one-off car using a technology around for many years and will not be coming to public roads in 2028,” said Smith, a law professor at the University of South Carolina. “Tesla pretty uniquely has been able to sell itself on a future that is an order of magnitude greater than reality.”

Musk has repeatedly said that the future of driving will be autonomous -- and Austin-based Tesla has focused much of its business on building out self-driving features for its vehicles and, more recently, launching its own (still limited) robotaxi business.

But the company maintains that the Roadster will be made to have humans behind the wheel, calling the EV the “best of the last human-driven cars.”

Thursday’s demo was technically autonomous “to make sure we don’t kill anyone,” Musk noted. But long-term, he said, the new Roadster will be “the only manually driven car that Tesla makes.”

“This is not necessarily a safety-optimized car,” Musk later added, met by laughter from the audience. But “it takes the fun meter to 11 out of 10.”

Tesla’s first Roadster was launched back in 2008. And in 2018, Musk went as far as placing one on a rocket -- with a mannequin dubbed “Starman” in the driver’s seat -- and launching it into space.

Again, the second-generation Roadster isn’t immediately hitting the market. And whether the ambitious new vehicle boosts the company’s bottom line remains to be seen.

In second-quarter earnings reported over the summer, Tesla’s profits fell as the company spent more on research and development for its robotaxi and robotics businesses -- which cut into money made from an otherwise sharp increase in vehicle sales. Net income totalled US$1.11 billion for the period, while revenue climbed to $28.24 billion.

The Associated Press

items.title: Metro Vancouver home prices drop 4% in Q3 as Royal LePage forecasts further decline
items.description: Trade uncertainty keeps Metro Vancouver homebuyers on sidelines, says the brokage
items._ogDesc: Trade uncertainty keeps Metro Vancouver homebuyers on sidelines, says the brokage
items.body:
Metro Vancouver home prices continued to fall in the third quarter as economic uncertainty and concerns about future borrowing costs kept buyers on the sidelines, according to a new report from Royal LePage.

The aggregate home price in Metro Vancouver, which tracks price trends across different types of homes, declined four per cent year-over-year and 1.4 per cent from the previous quarter in the third quarter of 2026, according to the brokerage’s latest House Price Survey and Market Forecast, released Oct. 15.

Royal LePage forecasts the region’s aggregate home price will fall a further 4.5 per cent year-over-year in the fourth quarter.

“The Vancouver housing market hasn’t come to a total standstill, but it is operating well below normal levels, with transaction volumes consistently running 25 to 30 per cent below our 10-year average,” said Randy Ryalls, managing broker at Royal LePage Sterling Realty, in a statement.

“Sales activity steadily declined over the summer months and into the start of fall, and while inventory tightened slightly, it hasn't been enough to keep prices from declining.”

The median price of a single-family detached home in Metro Vancouver fell 5.6 per cent year-over-year to nearly $1.62 million, while the median condo price declined 4.1 per cent year-over-year to $712,100.

Nationally, the aggregate home price fell 0.8 per cent year-over-year to $810,000, while the median condo price declined 1.5 per cent to $571,900.

Phil Soper, Royal LePage president and CEO, said renewed trade tensions between Canada and the U.S. have weighed on consumer confidence, making prospective buyers more hesitant to commit to major purchases.

Concerns that mortgage rates could rise are also keeping would-be buyers on the sidelines, he added.

“The opportunity is there; the confidence to act remains elusive,” said Soper in a statement.

“With more homes to choose from and little pressure to act quickly, buyers can afford to wait—and uncertainty gives them a reason to.”

According to Royal LePage’s 2026 Mortgage Renewal Survey, 45 per cent of Vancouver homeowners with a mortgage on their primary residence expect their monthly payments to increase when they renew.

Household debt is adding to financial pressures, as non-mortgage debt reached $712.2 billion in the second quarter, up 4.8 per cent year-over-year, according to figures cited in the report.

“It’s created a stop-and-start environment, where momentum never really takes off and pricing strategy is everything,” said Ryalls, adding that some sellers are pulling properties off the market if they’re not desperate to sell, while homes that are “aggressively priced” still attract multiple offers.

Despite forecasting a further decline in Metro Vancouver, Royal LePage expects Canada’s aggregate home price to increase one per cent year-over-year in the fourth quarter of 2026.

items._ogDesc: Canadian real estate demand just hit its weakest September level since 1994, spending almost 5 years to wipe out just 13 months of gains.
items.body:
Canadian real estate prices slid further, spending almost 5 years to wipe out just 13 months of gains. Canadian Real Estate Association (CREA) data shows home sales fell further in September. Falling demand and lofty inventory left the weakest September demand balance since 1994.

Canadian Home Prices Have Spent Nearly 5 Years Wiping Out 13 Months of Gains

Canadian real estate prices: The price of a typical home across Canada (composite benchmark).

Source: CREA; Better Dwelling.

The price of a typical home dropped for a fourth straight month, falling 0.9% (-$5.7k) to $651,400 in September. That’s 3.4% (-$22.7k) lower than last year, and currently sits at its lowest level since February 2021. It’s a timeline that really highlights how bizarre the initial surge was.

Canadian home prices peaked in March 2022, falling 22.5% (-$189.0k) as of last month. The drop is big, but the 54-month correction only wiped out gains from February 2021 to March 2022. A 13-month rise with the pandemic’s almost zero population growth took almost 5 years to correct. The demand balance also indicates that prices are still a little too steep.

Canadian Real Estate Sales Slip, Inventory Remains Lofty

Canadian home sales through the MLS vs new listings for September.

Source: CREA; Better Dwelling.

A backslide in demand is clearly one of the reasons that prices are pulling back. There were 36,657 existing homes sold through the MLS in September, 7.7% fewer than last year. CREA has only reported weaker September sales 3 times in the past 10 years: 2023, 2022, and 2018. The initial correction explains the weak volumes in 2022 and 2023, while 2018’s slump was during the initial rollout of Ontario’s foreign buyer tax. However, there was a big difference last month—inventory.

Canadian Real Estate Demand Balance At Weakest Level Since 1994

National sales to new listings ratio (SNLR) for September.

Source: CREA; Better Dwelling.

There were a whopping 88,186 new listings that hit the market last month. It was 5.4% lower than last year, but remains the second most new listings in September on record. Last year may have been higher, but weaker home sales eroded the demand balance further. The sales-to-new-listings ratio (SNLR) fell to 41.6%, the weakest September since 1994—32 years ago.

Traditionally, analysts refer to an SNLR between 40% and 60% as a balanced market. However, CREA’s updated guidance considers 45% to 65% balanced at the national level. According to the new guidance, we’re in a buyer’s market where prices are expected to fall further.

Last year, a mild improvement in sales had much of the industry forecasting a recovery this year. RBC even declared the bottom of the market—it was the 8th time in 4 years, but it still resonated with the industry. After the first 9 months of 2026, the industry may be ready to change its tune. This morning, CREA released its latest guidance showing downward revisions to its forecast.

items.title: EverWind says $10B AI data centre proposal largest private investment in N.S. history
items.description: A company pursuing an ambitious wind and hydrogen development in Nova Scotia says it now has plans for a $10-billion AI data centre in Cape Breton.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[EverWind CEO, Trent Vichie, is seen making the announcement in Port Tupper, N.S. (CTV/Ryan MacDonald)]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: A company pursuing an ambitious wind and hydrogen development in Nova Scotia says it now has plans for a $10-billion AI data centre in Cape Breton.
items.body:
POINT TUPPER — A company pursuing a wind and hydrogen development in Nova Scotia says it has plans for a $10-billion AI data centre in Cape Breton that it describes as the largest private investment in provincial history.

EverWind Fuels announced Friday that U.S. AI company Anthropic has signed a 20-year lease for a 18,600-square metre data centre in Point Tupper, N.S., that would draw 95 megawatts of electricity during its first phase.

EverWind officials declined to disclose the value of the lease with the company, which says the site will power its Claude AI assistant and growing Canadian demand. Anthropic, led by CEO Dario Amodei, said in a press release that Canada is the sixth-largest user of Claude worldwide.

The data centre is scheduled to come online late next year. A 325-megawatt expansion is expected in mid-2028, which would bring the development’s total energy demand to 420 megawatts, the company said.

“Speed matters, and capable partners matter and this is something that we can do,” Vichie told a news conference in Point Tupper. “We can set an example for the rest of the country on how we can bring this industry to Canada and to protect Canadian sovereignty.”

The plan includes $8 billion to build a data centre campus and $2 billion to advance onshore wind energy projects. The company said the project will create 2,000 construction jobs and 215 permanent positions.

Permanent data centre jobs will pay between $135,000 and $185,000 per year, and the project will create millions of dollars in spinoff benefits, the company said.

Vichie, who is based in New York, launched EverWind about four years ago to build wind and green hydrogen projects in Atlantic Canada. He was previously a senior managing director and co-founder at New York alternative investment firm Stonepeak Infrastructure Partners. Prior to that, he was a senior managing director at alternative investor The Blackstone Group and a managing director at Australia’s Macquarie Bank.

Vichie said EverWind is still pursuing its hydrogen development at Point Tupper. He said the hydrogen and data centre projects will compliment each other as both are expected to be powered by Nova Scotia’s abundant renewable wind resources.

“You often hear that Canada is a resource economy, (but) it’s also an intellectual economy,” Vichie said.

“And we need this type of investment to support that part of the equation. They both play off each other very well, resources and knowledge. And Canadians have that in spades.”

EverWind plans to spend its own capital on the data centre, and with a long-term lease in place, will now pursue financing from banks and pension plans.

Premier Tim Houston said the data centre project was a major vote of confidence in the rural area about 200 kilometres east of Halifax. He said Canada does not have enough secure data infrastructure to meet the requirements of its businesses, governments and health-care institutions.

“This represents the connection between the high-technology possibilities and potential of our province, and the energy generation potential that we have,” said Houston, who is also promoting an ambitious $60-billion offshore wind project called Wind West.

Data centres are typically massive operations that require immense amounts of electricity to run and cool off computer servers.

Water from nearby Landrie Lake will be used to cool the Point Tupper data centre’s servers, and the company stressed it will safeguard the water supply.

EverWind said the cooling system will be closed-loop, similar to a car’s radiator, with cooling fluid recycled or disposed of off site, not in local waterways. The system will use an average of 100,000 litres of water per day in the first phase, which EverWind said is about the same as a large shopping mall.

That will expand to an average draw of 500,000 litre per day when the expansion is complete, about one per cent of the lake’s safe daily yield of 34 million litres.

The firm already has environmental approvals for four wind farms in mainland Nova Scotia with capacity to produce 650 megawatts of power. A consortium of First Nations, led by the Membertou First Nation in Cape Breton, own 51 per cent of those projects.

The company has begun preliminary construction work at some sites. And three more wind farms are in the planning stages.

The company said negotiations are underway with the Membertou Development Corporation to take a nine per cent equity stake in the data centre project. As well, the company says it’s planning extensive public consultations.

EverWind said its wind farms won’t be ready by the time the data centre is expected to open in late 2027, but company officials said the province’s independent grid operator has produced a study saying existing energy infrastructure can support the operation.

The company plans to build about 200 megawatt-hours of battery storage at the site.

On another front, EverWind confirmed it will pay the full cost of all energy connections, network upgrades and other costs associated with the data centre project so they are not passed on to existing Nova Scotia ratepayers.

EverWind has signed on to the federal government’s responsible data centre principles and says it has agreed to meet provincial conditions as well.

Houston suggested Friday that his government doesn’t plan to legislate new data centre rules, instead pointing to existing environmental and industrial approval processes.

NDP Opposition Leader Claudia Chender issued a statement Friday calling on Houston to protect the public from power rate shocks from data centres.

“The Houston government is supporting this project without any discussion, consultation, legislation or regulations,” Chender said. “The premier is saying people should just trust his word that Nova Scotians will be protected.”

Earlier this year, Houston said it was premature to discuss potential data centres until major projects such as Wind West were completed. He softened that stance last month saying data centres could help create demand and investment cases for energy projects.

The project is the latest in a string of data centre projects popping up across the country.

In March, BCE Inc. announced plans for a 300-megawatt site just outside Regina, which the company increased to 1.2 gigawatts last month. In May, Telus and the federal government announced three data centres in B.C., while Meta, the parent company of Facebook, announced in July a $13-billion, one-gigawatt AI data centre north of Edmonton.

Meanwhile, opposition to data centres has been rising in communities across Canada.

In late June, protesters rallied in Vancouver to protest the opening of AI data centres.

Earlier that month, Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew said no to a massive data centre southeast of Winnipeg, citing the sheer size of the project and its potential threat to the environment.

In August, the Alberta Utilities Commission has denied an application to build a 1.4-gigawatt natural gas plant that would have powered a massive data centre complex in the small town of Olds, Alta.

The Ontario communities of Oakville and Mississauga, Ont., recently passed one-year moratoriums on data centre development.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 16, 2026.

-- By Devin Stevens in Halifax.

items.title: Fraud probe and family rift tighten grip on former MP
items.description: Police, Ontario’s law regulator and politician's father-in-law allege more than $200m in fraud
items.content: <p>Police, Ontario’s law regulator and politician's father-in-law allege more than $200m in fraud</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639277625591149616.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Police, Ontario’s law regulator and politician's father-in-law allege more than $200m in fraud
items.body:
Rajvinder “Raj” Grewal, the former Liberal member of Parliament for Brampton East, Ontario, is under simultaneous legal siege from Peel Regional Police, the Law Society of Ontario (LSO), and his own father-in-law — all over alleged misconduct at RSG Law, the Mississauga firm he founded.

Civil disputes against Grewal and associates exceed $200 million, according to recently filed lawsuits. None of the allegations has been established in court.

From Parliament to police probe

Grewal represented Brampton East from 2015 to 2019, resigning from the Liberal caucus that year after admitting to gambling debts of several million dollars. He founded RSG Law shortly after, a firm a 2025 paid advertorial in the Toronto Star called a “thriving legal enterprise.”

Earlier this year, Grewal voluntarily surrendered his law licence as the LSO launched a formal investigation into alleged mortgage and trust fund misconduct, coming amid Ontario’s escalating enforcement actions against mortgage fraud in 2025 and 2026.

In September, the regulator escalated further, filing to seize all RSG Law accounts, client files, and safe-deposit boxes. Only $340,303 remains in the firm’s accounts, according to the LSO’s notice of application.

Peel Regional Police confirmed on October 9, a criminal investigation into “multiple” allegations of fraud and breach of trust at RSG Law, part of Ontario’s mounting mortgage fraud and trust account enforcement actions.

Grewal’s lawyer Simon Bieber maintains his client denies wrongdoing, is co-operating with the LSO, and “looks forward to continuing his defence,” adding that Grewal is “working diligently to resolve all outstanding litigation in a manner that is fair to all involved.”

Receivership and a father-in-law’s allegations

The legal crisis has also engulfed Grewal’s real estate arm. RSG Mayfield Inc., of which he is sole director and officer, was placed into receivership after defaulting on a $26,269,753.66 loan secured against an undeveloped Mayfield Road residential site, according to Insolvency Insider Canada.

Financed in 2025 by Vector Financial Services Limited and Olympia Trust Company, a court has since appointed TDB Restructuring to manage the sale.

The affair has also divided Grewal’s family. Father-in-law Kailash Kasal, a Brampton businessman, swore an affidavit on September 25, alleging Grewal used his companies and properties to fraudulently secure tens of millions in mortgage loans without his knowledge.

Kasal states the electronic signatures on mortgage documents purporting to be his were not his, and that an ink signature attributed to his wife was “a clear forgery.”

He has since cross-sued Grewal, Davinder Singh Khattra — RSG Law’s listed new owner, whose licence has also been suspended — and RSG Law itself, seeking $1 million in damages for “negligent and/or fraudulent misrepresentation.”

The LSO’s application references lawsuits alleging at least $17 million misappropriated from RSG Law client accounts, while National Bank of Canada is separately seeking $4.1 million in allegedly diverted mortgage funds.

In a June ruling in that case, Ontario Superior Court Justice Frederick Myers found the “funds are unaccounted for and appear to have been misappropriated by the defendants.”

items.title: Former Ontario mortgage broker settles unlicensed fronting case
items.description: Regulator trims penalty as broker admits relying on an unlicensed referrer to vet borrowers
items.content: <p>Regulator trims penalty as broker admits relying on an unlicensed referrer to vet borrowers</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639277602168654143.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Regulator trims penalty as broker admits relying on an unlicensed referrer to vet borrowers
items.body:
A former Ontario mortgage broker who let an unlicensed referral agent handle her client intake has agreed to pay $40,000 to the Financial Services Regulatory Authority of Ontario (FSRA), settling a case in which the regulator had sought more than twice that amount.

Paramjeet Kaur, whose broker licence through Trillium Mortgage Services Inc. expired on March 31, admitted to six breaches of the Mortgage Brokerages, Lenders and Administrators Act, 2006 and its regulations, including facilitating illegal conduct and giving lenders false or deceptive information.

The order, dated Sept. 24, replaces the $85,000 in penalties FSRA proposed in April. The final figure is about 47% of that amount.

How the unlicensed referral pipeline worked

The case began with a May 1, 2024, complaint from a borrower, identified as MA, who said the mortgage registered on her Hamilton property was higher than the amount she had agreed to. She told investigators she had never met Kaur and did not know Trillium was her brokerage.

According to the agreed facts, Vatsal Pareshkumar Khamar, also known as Vic Kumar, answered a Kijiji ad Kaur placed in 2023 and began referring clients to her.

Khamar, who has never held a licence, met eight groups of borrowers, collected their identification and financial documents and obtained signatures.

Kaur prepared the applications and sent them to lenders through Trillium. She relied on Khamar to confirm the borrowers’ identities and never met any of them in person.

Kaur admitted listing one borrower as single when she was married, supplying inaccurate employment and income details for that borrower and overstating MA’s income.

FSRA’s April notice said she knew MA was a low-income college student and earned approximately $90,000 in commissions on the files. Trillium collected roughly $11,000.

“Kaur knew that Khamar was unlicensed, and yet relied on him to complete some of the fundamental obligations of a Mortgage Broker and facilitated his conduct,” the notice said.

She also answered “No” on a March 2025 renewal application asking whether she was under investigation. That was months after FSRA sent her an inquiry letter.

The notice further alleged that typed notes she submitted as 2023 records had metadata showing they were created on Feb. 1.

What the case signals for Ontario mortgage brokers

The regulator’s April proposal against Trillium and three others also targeted the brokerage and its principal broker. It sought $60,000 from Trillium and $25,000 from principal broker Frank Manzo. It sought $80,000 and a compliance order against Khamar.

All four parties asked for hearings before the Financial Services Tribunal, and the allegations against the remaining three have not been proven. Kaur has undertaken to testify at a hearing on the merits. 

The case resembles FSRA’s decision to revoke Expert Financial Corporation’s brokerage licence over unlicensed activity. It also fits the trend in FSRA’s first enforcement annual report for 2024–25, which recorded 100 enforcement actions, up from 65 the previous year. 

“They’re finally taking seriously the role we play as mortgage professionals in the transaction. It’s frustrating to see the lack of professionalism [from some mortgage agents]. But I think what the latest regulation is doing is making the good ones even better and the bad ones are that much more obvious,” Joe Sammut, broker of record at Mortgage Architects, told Canadian Mortgage Professional earlier this year.

FSRA said Khamar’s conduct left borrowers without the Act’s protections, including errors and omissions insurance. Joe White, founder and CEO of REMIC, made a similar point about licensing at MortgageFest Canada 2026, while discussing AI tools.

“Brokers are licensed. AI isn’t. The fact that brokers have errors and omissions insurance so that if something goes wrong, the client’s protected,” White said.

At the same event, Andy Kuyper, head of partnerships and secured lending at TransUnion, warned that the risk will grow as volumes recover.

“Fraud is a problem. It’s far easier for fraud to be committed when times are busy and everyone’s busy. So right now we’re in a good spot, but I would caution the industry to be careful as this industry rebounds – to be hypervigilant on fraud,” Kuyper said.

items.title: Suspended Markham brokerage kept dealing, Ontario regulator alleges
items.description: Alleged repeat disclosure failures could keep a Markham principal broker out of the business
items.content: <p>Alleged repeat disclosure failures could keep a Markham principal broker out of the business</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639277586609719389.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Alleged repeat disclosure failures could keep a Markham principal broker out of the business
items.body:
The Financial Services Regulatory Authority of Ontario (FSRA) is moving to keep Renkai Lin out of the province’s mortgage brokering sector and to revoke the licence of his Markham brokerage, ZK Financial Inc.

The regulator alleges the pair kept arranging mortgages while suspended and gave it false information again, about a year after settling a similar case.

In a notice of proposal dated Sept. 2, Troy Harrison, FSRA’s acting director of litigation and enforcement, proposed refusing Lin’s April 9, application to reinstate his mortgage broker licence and revoking ZK Financial’s brokerage licence.

The notice said Lin, the brokerage’s principal broker and sole director, has shown “a pattern of unwillingness to comply with the requirements of the Act and regulations.”

The allegations have not been proven, and Lin and ZK Financial have requested a hearing before the Financial Services Tribunal.

A second round after a 2025 settlement

Lin held a licence from 2018 until May 8, 2025. ZK Financial was incorporated federally in October 2020 and licensed in January 2021.

In October 2024, FSRA moved against both for failing to disclose criminal charges laid in June 2022. The charges were missing from their 2023 and 2024 renewal applications and from their Annual Information Returns (AIRs), the yearly filings brokerages submit to the regulator.

Under an April 25, 2025, settlement, Lin and the brokerage admitted providing false or misleading information. They agreed to a $6,000 administrative penalty and a suspension.

A May 8, 2025, order required Lin to personally verify that every filing was accurate. On May 22, 2025, he was charged with further criminal offences, which remain before the courts.

FSRA now alleges Lin breached that condition. His reinstatement application left out a civil claim, issued Dec. 8, 2025, over brokerage fees on a mortgage renewal.

The regulator said he also left the lawsuit off the 2025 AIR, and that the 2024 and 2025 returns omitted mortgage and fee information he admitted in that proceeding.

Undisclosed proceedings have cost other licences. FSRA cited an inaccurate civil-proceedings declaration when it refused to renew the licence of broker Joel Kelman.

It also turned down a former principal broker who applied while criminal charges were outstanding, when it denied a broker licence to former Monarch Mortgage principal Victor Peca. 

What does the deposit rule mean for brokers?

FSRA says that between April 29 and June 1, ZK Financial took on a borrower while Lin was unlicensed and the brokerage was suspended. The notice identifies the borrower only as ZY and says the brokerage worked to arrange a mortgage of between $100,000 and $280,000.

According to the notice, Lin took a $2,000 deposit for his services and later refused to return it. Ontario Regulation 188/08 bars brokerages from requiring advance payments on mortgages of $400,000 or less.

FSRA also alleges that, during the suspension, ZK Financial’s website and 51.ca listings presented it as arranging a high volume of mortgages, which contradicted its 2025 AIR.

The regulator has drawn this line before. “Licensees must not facilitate activities for unlicensed individuals,” said Elissa Sinha, FSRA’s director of litigation and enforcement, when the regulator revoked the brokerage licence of Expert Financial Corporation. 

At MortgageFest Canada 2026, held in Toronto in September, Joe White, founder and chief executive of the Real Estate and Mortgage Institute of Canada (REMIC), argued that the licence itself is a broker’s core protection for clients. 

“Brokers are licensed. AI isn’t. The fact that brokers have errors and omissions insurance so that if something goes wrong, the client’s protected. AI can’t do that,” he said.

“What consumers will understand over time is that what they get with dealing with a broker is competency, and that takes years to create.”

Under Ontario Regulation 410/07, principal brokers must take reasonable steps to keep their brokerages compliant. FSRA alleges Lin failed to meet that duty.

The notice does not set a hearing date.

items.title: Expert: Canada’s Homes Got Cheaper In September, But Buyers Still Pulled Back
items.description:
Canadian homes got cheaper in September. Buyers responded by purchasing fewer of them. A falling price is welcome, but it does little for a household whose mortgage approval no longer covers the home.

There were 36,657 residential sales in September, 7.7% fewer than a year earlier. Sales fell 2.3% from August after seasonal adjustment, so the decline went beyond the usual seasonal change.

September residential sales, not seasonally adjusted; the annual comparison uses CREA’s revised figures. Chart: valery.ca · Data: CREA.

The national benchmark price fell 0.4% during September and was 3.4% below a year earlier. The average sale price fell 1.6% annually to $666,538. The benchmark tracks comparable housing attributes; the average also changes with the mix of homes sold.

Annual changes in the unadjusted national MLS® HPI and average sale price. The average is affected by the mix of transactions. Chart: valery.ca · Data: CREA.

A discount can disappear into the mortgage

CREA blames the weaker outlook on another increase in fixed mortgage rates and uncertainty over how far variable rates may rise. Its October forecast points to renewed energy-related inflation risks and a more hawkish Bank of Canada. The assumption of an easy return to cheaper borrowing has become harder to defend.

A buyer can negotiate thousands off the purchase price and still face a payment they cannot carry. How much of the discount survives depends on the mortgage size, rate and amortization. The asking price has come down; the lender has not necessarily become more generous.

There is more scope to negotiate than there was during the boom, but national listings are hardly overflowing. CREA counted slightly more than 200,000 homes for sale at the end of September, up just 1.8% annually and close to the historical norm.

B.C.’s supply problem looks different from Manitoba’s

Canada had 4.9 months of inventory after seasonal adjustment. British Columbia had 7.0 months, Manitoba 2.4, and Saskatchewan 3.4. Ontario was at 4.7. The ratio compares the stock of listings with the current sales pace.

Seasonally adjusted residential months of inventory by province. Local property types can differ substantially. Chart: valery.ca · Data: CREA.

Ontario’s sales-to-new-listings ratio was only 41.9%, even with fewer months of inventory than B.C. The first ratio compares purchases with new listings arriving that month. Months of inventory compares the stock already available with the current sales pace.

A buyer shopping for an apartment can face much less competition than someone looking for a detached home in the same city. Provincial totals are a poor substitute for checking the homes that actually fit the budget.

Ontario is doing worse than the national forecast

CREA forecasts a 0.2% increase in the national annual average sale price to $681,681 in 2026. Ontario’s average is forecast to fall 3% to $809,334, and B.C.’s to fall 0.8%. Gains elsewhere keep the national number slightly positive.

Ontario and B.C. are the two provinces with forecast annual average-price declines in 2026. Chart: valery.ca · Data: CREA.

Newfoundland and Labrador has the strongest expected average-price growth this year at 5.7%, followed by Saskatchewan at 5%. CREA expects both to slow in 2027, to 3.1% and 2.5% respectively.

The national average is projected to reach $689,909 in 2027, up 1.2%. Ontario’s forecast gain is 0.7%, to $815,100. These are nominal annual averages. Ontario’s projected increase next year would recover only a small part of this year’s forecast loss.

Annual average transaction prices in Canadian dollars. Forecast values are not December price targets. Chart: valery.ca · Data: CREA.

Five years later, parts of Ontario are still cheaper

Greater Toronto’s September benchmark was 14.7% below its September 2021 level. Hamilton-Burlington was down 15.3%. Calgary was 24.6% higher, Quebec City 54.4% higher and St. John’s 41.2% higher. These are seasonally adjusted composite benchmarks measured from September 2021, before the 2022 peak.

Five-year changes in seasonally adjusted composite MLS® HPI benchmarks, September 2021 to September 2026. Chart: valery.ca · Data: CREA.

For an owner in one of the weaker Ontario markets, waiting has already failed to guarantee a better sale price. Moving can mean accepting less equity than expected while financing the next purchase at a higher rate. That is a good reason for a household to stay put, even when it would rather move.

Developers also have to compete with the prices buyers can pay for existing homes. Softer resale prices can squeeze the revenue available to cover a new project’s costs. CREA’s releases do not track presales, construction costs, or developer balance sheets, so they cannot tell us which projects will proceed.

Pent-up demand still needs a mortgage

CREA now expects 444,530 sales in 2026 and 464,235 in 2027. The forecast rebound of 4.4% would leave annual sales 4,436 below 2025. Even the recovery scenario falls short of that earlier year’s activity.

The confident pitch about pent-up demand has become harder to hear over repeated forecast cuts. CREA still uses the term in its 2027 outlook, but buyers are expected to return after economic growth, renewed population growth and a clearer interest-rate path help them along. Calling demand pent-up does not make it financeable.

That forecast also assumes limited further action by the Bank of Canada. September showed how quickly higher borrowing costs can interrupt a recovery. Buyers may get a better price this fall, but they still have to live with the payment.


CREA’s September 2026 monthly statistics and MLS® HPI package and October 2026 housing forecast, released October 16, 2026. Statistics retain the comparisons and revisions in the supplied media PDFs. Annual forecast prices are nominal transaction averages; forecasts are scenarios, not observed outcomes.

Monthly statistics: https://stats.crea.ca/en-ca/

Quarterly forecasts (October media PDF; July comparison uses the official July 15 vintage): https://www.crea.ca/housing-market-stats/canadian-housing-market-stats/quarterly-forecasts/

Charts: valery.ca · Data: CREA. MLS® and Multiple Listing Service® are CREA trademarks. Independent analysis; no CREA affiliation or endorsement.

items.description: Rate-hike jitters are pushing buyers to the sidelines as the Canadian housing market braces for a slower end to the year
items.content: <p>Rate-hike jitters are pushing buyers to the sidelines as the Canadian housing market braces for a slower end to the year</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639277543854804701.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Rate-hike jitters are pushing buyers to the sidelines as the Canadian housing market braces for a slower end to the year
items.body:
The Canadian Real Estate Association (CREA) has lowered its home sales forecast for a third straight quarter, now projecting 444,530 residential transactions through Multiple Listing Service® (MLS®) Systems.

That would be a 5.2% drop from 2025, as rising fixed mortgage rates and the threat of a Bank of Canada hike sideline buyers.

The October 16 revision strips 18,806 sales from CREA’s July estimate, when the association expected a far milder 1.4% annual decline in home sales.

The national average price is now forecast to edge up just 0.2% to $681,681, roughly $5,000 below the summer call.

How rising fixed mortgage rates hit September home sales

CREA said oil prices began climbing again in early September while the Bank of Canada struck a more hawkish tone, with markets now pricing in approximately 100 basis points of hikes by this time next year.

The five-year Government of Canada bond yield, which lenders use to price fixed mortgages, closed at 3.60% on October 2, up from 3.35% on September 1.

September sales fell 2.3% from August and 7.7% from a year earlier. The national average sale price was $666,538, down 1.6% year over year.

Lenders saw the repricing coming.

“I think rates will probably go up in October. GIC rates are up 35 points in the last sixty to ninety days. Bank of Canada bond rates are up 60 points. Like everything’s been going up already. So it’s just a natural part of the market,” Grant Armstrong, chief growth officer at WealthOne Bank of Canada, said at MortgageFest Canada in Toronto in September.

Victor Tran, a mortgage agent at Tango Financial in Toronto, is already seeing borrowers rethink their options.

“The variable-rate forecast isn’t looking too good either,” Tran told Canadian Mortgage Professional as bond markets turned volatile in September.

“So we have people sitting in variable rates considering locking into fixed rates, for example.”

Tracy Valko, founder of AIMI Mortgage Collective, said brokers need to be able to explain those forces to clients.

“There’s a lot of global tensions right now that are affecting our market. What’s affecting bond yields? What affects fixed rates? Agents and brokers should know that. We as mortgage agents and brokers should never predict, but one thing we should do is make sure that we understand the knowledge so we can future-prepare homeowners for what could be coming down the pipeline,” Valko said at the event.

Ontario and BC weigh on 2026 home prices

CREA expects Ontario’s average price to fall 3% to $809,334 and British Columbia’s to slip 0.8% to $944,685 this year, while Newfoundland and Labrador (5.7%) and Saskatchewan (5%) lead gains.

For 2027, it forecasts a 4.4% rebound to 464,235 sales and a 1.2% price gain to $689,909, assuming limited action from the central bank. Even that recovery would leave sales about 4,400 below 2025 levels.

Andy Kuyper, head of partnerships and secured lending at TransUnion, was cautious on timing.

“I’d like to be optimistic. I think we’re facing the reality that with the geopolitical climate and everything that’s happening here, our mortgage industry is probably not ready to rebound. We are seeing slight growth in originations, we’re seeing slight growth in mortgage balances – a lot more on the refi side,” he said at MortgageFest.

Brokers say the slowdown raises the value of advice over price.

“Now more than ever it’s so important for people to use a mortgage broker rather than their bank, because the banks are specifically just focusing on rates. As we head into a turbulent time where potentially we will see an increase in rates, the banks are putting clients in, say, a variable rate, which may not be the best option for that client – just because it has a three in front of it,” said Sabeena Bubber, a mortgage broker at Xeva Mortgage.

Valko expects little relief. “The next two years are going to be very similar to what we’re dealing with right now. Staying a best-rate mortgage broker is not going to get you the goals that you want,” she said.

Dr. Sherry Cooper, chief economist at Dominion Lending Centres (DLC), expects a hike by late 2026 or the first half of 2027.

“We have to expect higher interest rates, which also means that fixed-rate mortgages are very attractive now,” she said.

The Bank of Canada’s next rate decision is October 28.

items.title: How credit unions are navigating a turbulent 2026 market
items.description: CEO spells out careful approach in a lending environment marked by risk and plenty of volatility
items.content: <p>CEO spells out careful approach in a lending environment marked by risk and plenty of volatility</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639276728476168839.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: CEO spells out careful approach in a lending environment marked by risk and plenty of volatility
items.body:
Canada’s current housing market is moribund, according to a leading community lending chief executive officer. And that means credit unions are navigating a difficult balancing act: maintaining volumes without taking on undue risk in a market where prices are still falling.

Fausto Gaudio, president and chief executive officer of the Toronto-headquartered IC Savings, described the current market as one where activity was barely getting off the ground. “It’s very, very soft,” he told Canadian Mortgage Professional. “Softer than it was last year – and last year was also a very soft year in terms of trades and prices declining as well.”

That marks one of the biggest obstacles facing credit unions and other lenders. Maintaining asset size is no easy feat, but loosening credit standards to bring more business in isn’t always the best idea either as values continue to slide.

“Top of mind is that there just isn’t enough volume,” Gaudio said. “It’s very, very difficult… to maintain asset size, because unless we expand our risk tolerance and do mortgages at a higher loan-to-value at a time when prices are declining. That’s a real challenge, especially for small boutique lenders.”

Gaudio said IC Savings has opted to hold its position rather than chase volume, steering clear of high-LTV lending. “We do very few mortgages at the 80% loan-to-value,” he said. “And so we don’t seem to have a lot of the problems that the big banks have in terms of defaults and powers of sale today.”

But there’s also opportunity in the market, not least in serving borrowers who fall outside standard bank approval criteria. Tighter lending standards among Canada’s banking giants mean borrowers often don’t qualify in the current market not because of recklessness, but rather circumstance.

When dealing with those customers, understanding the story – and the “why” of how their current situation developed – is crucial, according to Gaudio.

“With somebody that might have had a difficulty – having gone through a health problem, a period of unemployment, a marital breakup – we’re much more attentive to those human stories and try to resolve their problems,” he said.

“When a borrower is coming out of a life experience and a setback, we’re much more willing to try to resolve their issue – but at the same time, they need to have some equity to offset that risk.”

Reverse mortgages: Will their popularity grow in the credit union space?

Gaudio said IC Savings has developed a new term reverse mortgage, a fixed-period alternative to the traditional lifetime arrangement, aimed at homeowners who want to access equity but have a clear exit plan within a few years.

The product, he said, is for “someone that wants to live in their house another three or possibly five years, but then they have a plan – to move back to Northern Ontario or the East Coast where they had family or grandkids – but they don’t want to commit to a reverse mortgage for life.”

2027 outlook for wider market remains unclear

Gaudio sees the current housing market sluggishness as a product of rampant unaffordability rather than the geopolitical headwinds hovering over the Canadian economy.

Trade turmoil and rising oil prices, he said, have less impact of the housing market than the fact that prices have skyrocketed over the past decade, and remain elevated in many regions despite the years-long cooldown.

It remains unclear whether the broader market will normalize quickly enough to ease volume pressure on boutique lenders heading into 2027, but with borrower stress likely to continue rising, he emphasized the importance of brokers and agents telling their customer’s story in as much detail as possible to boost their chances of getting a deal through.

“I believe the brokers that deal with us know us as that type of lender,” he said.

items.title: What persistently high bond yields could mean for the commercial mortgage market
items.description: Avison Young flags cap rate pressure as lenders tighten underwriting on income properties
items.content: <p>Avison Young flags cap rate pressure as lenders tighten underwriting on income properties</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639276802996438662.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Avison Young flags cap rate pressure as lenders tighten underwriting on income properties
items.body:
Persistently high long-term bond yields are shaping up as the deciding variable for Canada’s commercial mortgage market, with Avison Young warning that capitalization rates may struggle to hold if borrowing costs stay elevated into 2027.

In its Q3 2026 Canadian cap rate and investment trends report, the real estate services firm said yields no longer move on central bank policy alone, with persistent inflation, government borrowing, trade disruptions, energy markets and geopolitical tension lifting financing costs and investors’ required returns.

The cap rate, a property’s net operating income divided by its value, is where that pressure lands. Higher cap rates mean lower valuations and smaller loans for income-property clients.

National benchmarks sat at 4.55% for high-density urban multifamily, 5.85% for new single-tenant industrial and 6.90% for downtown class A office in the third quarter, following a second quarter in which Toronto anchored Canada’s commercial real estate rebound.

The five-year Government of Canada bond yield closed at 3.60% on October 2, up from 3.35% on September 1, according to Bank of Canada data, extending an oil-fuelled bond selloff that pushed Canada’s 10-year yield to 3.9% in September. 

“Bond markets are essentially doing some of the Bank of Canada’s job for them,” RBC economist Carrie Freestone said on the bank’s The 10-Minute Take podcast, as bond yields are already repricing Canada’s fixed mortgage market.

How are lenders pricing commercial mortgage risk?

Credit is still flowing, but on tighter terms. Conventional multifamily loans price 130 to 200 basis points over the five-year Government of Canada yield.

Loans insured by Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) price 55 to 100 basis points over it, the survey said.

Office spreads run 150 to 250 basis points. Multifamily arrears are trending up, and CMHC-insured applications fell from the prior quarter.

“While capital remains available across all asset classes, uncertainty related to geopolitical tensions, trade disruption, and rising bond yields is beginning to reduce borrowing capacity and increase lender caution,” said Ron Dezman, senior vice-president, debt capital and advisory, at Avison Young in Edmonton.

"In the CMHC lending market, underwriting assumptions for rental growth and threshold interest rates are becoming more conservative as supply risk deepens across several markets."

What higher yields mean for brokers’ commercial clients

Private investors made 48% of third-quarter acquisitions worth $5 million or more, according to CoStar data in the report. Mortgage renewal or maturity ranked as the second-most common reason owners sold multifamily assets.

“For multifamily pricing, bond yields will be the dominant story for the remainder of 2026, as a persistence of higher yields will likely place upward pressure on cap rates, especially with the relatively flat near-term income growth expectations,” said Carey Buntain, principal, capital markets, at Avison Young in Vancouver.

Grant Armstrong, chief growth officer at WealthOne Bank of Canada, flagged the move at MortgageFest Canada in Toronto in September.

“I think rates will probably go up in October. GIC rates are up 35 points in the last sixty to ninety days. Bank of Canada bond rates are up 60 points. Like everything’s been going up already. So it’s just a natural part of the market,” Armstrong said.

The post Canadian Bond Yields & Borrowing Rates To Rise With US Inflation: BMO appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: Canadian bond yields are rising as hot US inflation is driving market expectations of four rate hikes from the Bank of Canada.
items.body:
The cross-border flow of goods is slow, but Canada’s imports of American inflation are ramping up. Government of Canada (GoC) short-term bond yields have climbed sharply since February. Gas prices were behind the initial surge, but yields are still climbing after gas stalled. A new report from BMO Capital Markets attributes the continued rise to hot U.S. inflation. The bank warns that markets are pricing in a full point of rate hikes from the Bank of Canada (BoC) by the end of 2027.

Canadian Bond Yields Pushed Higher By Hot U.S. Inflation

Higher gas prices have driven Canadian bond yields (and inflation) higher since February. BoC Governor Tiff Macklem warned yesterday that “every major central bank is worried…” because “…these costs have to go somewhere,” highlights BMO chief economist Douglas Porter.

Porter’s research shows the GoC 2-year bond yield’s correlation with gas prices at r=0.8, 1.0 being a perfect correlation. Gas prices and bond yields are moving very closely together, with the divergence only starting in September. Gas prices stabilized that month, but Canadian short- and medium-term yields rose further.

Porter flags the strong US jobs report as the catalyst that month. It was followed by a US Federal Reserve speech at Jackson Hole that was hawkish, suggesting the economy is running too hot. American inflation reported yesterday reinforced those concerns, as annual growth hit 3.7% in September, well above the 2% target.

Canadian yields are responding to that pressure, in addition to the energy bump. “Accordingly, the warm U.S. CPI has bumped Canadian yields again, with 2s backing up to 3.25%,” warns Porter.

Markets Expect Canadian Rates Will Rise 1 Point

Canada’s 2-year government bond yield hit 3.25% this week, reflecting expectations of tighter monetary policy. “That’s a full 100 bps above overnight rates, and the market is indeed expecting that much tightening by end-2027,” explains Porter.

The aggressive rise means higher mortgage rates may be ahead. A full point added to the overnight rate would trickle directly into variable rates. Fixed-rate mortgages are driven by bond yields, meaning they’re likely to lead here. BMO questions whether that much tightening is warranted while tariffs and trade uncertainty weigh on Canada. “That seems like a lot,” bluntly states Porter.

BMO Questions Scale of Tightening Amid Weak Economy

The market may be pricing in higher rates, but Canada’s economy may not be able to handle them. “Now, GoC yields are being largely pulled by domestic data—the weak jobs data helped pull them lower—and U.S. yields,” explains Porter.

Porter isn’t dismissing rate hikes, but suggests that market expectations are inflated. Higher rates would throttle demand, reducing inflation further. However, there’s still the matter of currency value that Porter doesn’t address. The situation the BoC faces is a little more complicated than just a demand issue.

Global commodities such as oil, wheat, and corn are generally priced in US dollars. That’s even the case for Canadian oil, which is priced based on global demand. Weak consumption can cool domestic price pressure, but a weaker loonie can still raise import costs. If hot US inflation keeps American rates elevated while Canadian weakness calls for relief, the BoC faces a difficult trade-off. A policy miss could deepen the slowdown or prolong inflation, raising stagflation risks.

Canadians are slightly happier with their banks this year, but the gain hides a loyalty problem that could reshape where younger borrowers take their business.

Overall customer satisfaction rose 3 points on a 1,000-point scale, lifted mainly by the Big 5 banks, according to the JD Power 2026 Canada Retail Banking Satisfaction Study.

However, fintechs – newer online banks – outscored both the Big 5 and midsize banks on many factors that drive satisfaction, and they are drawing a disproportionate share of younger Canadians planning to move their primary banking relationship.

Among Gen Z and Gen Y customers of traditional retail banks, 17% said they probably or definitely will switch primary banks within 12 months, a five-year high.

Four of the five leading reasons involve product offerings such as fees, interest rates and promotions.

“Younger customers can be satisfied with their bank and still leave if they see a better opportunity to save money elsewhere,” said Paul McAdam, senior director of banking and payments intelligence at JD Power.

“When household budgets are tight, a monthly banking fee becomes an expense worth reconsidering.”

RBC ranked highest among the Big 5 for a third straight year at 619. BMO and CIBC tied for second at 611, with TD close behind in fourth at 610.

Among midsize banks, Tangerine Bank took the top spot for a 15th consecutive year at 676, followed by ATB Financial at 650.

Why are younger bank customers ready to leave?

The findings echo an Equifax Canada survey showing most mortgage holders would consider switching lenders at renewal. Tracy Valko, founder of AIMI Mortgage Collective, described the financial strain behind that restlessness at MortgageFest Canada in Toronto in September.

“One out of two Canadians are $200 away from not meeting their financial obligations every month. And that’s profound. We never had this before. And they need that empathy – to see as a mortgage broker that you care about that,” she said.

The Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI) says frontier AI is among the fastest-growing threats facing lenders, warning that advanced models can help adversaries identify and exploit vulnerabilities at greater speed and scale. https://t.co/B9plArK6ju — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 12, 2026

What the bank switching trend means for mortgage brokers

A client willing to leave a bank over a monthly fee is a client willing to shop at renewal. Valko, who joined MortgageFest Canada’s Day 1 panel on the path forward for brokers, said winning that client takes more than price.

“As an industry, we got away from where it was about transactions and how many deals you did. Now it’s about focusing on that financial plan and strategy for that client, building that long-term financial relationship. So you look like a true expert and not just a rate agent.”

Prakash Bector, vice-president of national sales and distribution at EQ Bank, sees the opening.

"It's just staying focused on what we have in our control. So from a broker standpoint, it's those consistent outreaches to clients, leveraging your database, building new referral sources," she said during the mortgage event.

“As challenging as the market is, there’s immense opportunity for brokers. I think brokers’ share will continue to grow. A lot of clients need sound advice right now – they’re struggling, they don’t know what’s going to happen next. And this is where brokers play a critical role.”

Technology is part of that pitch, though not as advice. Fraud prevention and data security topped customers’ preferred uses of bank AI at 31%, against 12% for personal financial advice, a useful signal for brokers weighing how mortgage professionals can keep up with AI.

JD Power surveyed 14,038 retail banking customers in two waves during 2026.
